tip: Some verbs need a fixed preposition: ‘sylwi ar’ = to notice, literally notice on. ‘sylwodd e ddim ar y camgymeriad’.
‘pêl’ is feminine, so it soft-mutates after the definite article: ‘taflodd e’r bêl’ = he threw the ball, from ‘pêl’.
Welsh has no all-purpose word for no; you echo the verb. ‘nac ydy’ answers an ‘ydy’ question in the negative.
their brackets the noun as ‘eu ... nhw’: ‘eu gardd nhw’ means their garden, with ‘nhw’ reinforcing ‘eu’.
‘wedi’ plus a verb makes the had-done past: ‘doedd hi ddim wedi clywed’ = she had not heard.
‘trafferth’ is feminine, so it soft-mutates after the article ‘y’: ‘y drafferth’ means the trouble.
‘wedi’r cyfan’ is a set phrase meaning after all, used to open a concluding thought.
‘neb’ means anyone in a negative sentence and no one otherwise: here ‘ddim’ plus ‘neb’ = did not plus anyone.
‘eisiau’ (want) skips the usual ‘yn’: you say ‘ddim eisiau’, never ‘ddim yn eisiau’.
The negative past of ‘cael’ starts with ch: ‘ces’ becomes ‘ches’, so ‘ches i ddim’ means I didn’t get.
as ... as is ‘mor ... ag’: ‘mor syml ag’ means as simple as.
‘ei’ (her) leaves ‘gardd’ unchanged and pairs with ‘hi’; ‘ei’ (his) would soft-mutate it to ‘ardd’. So ‘ei gardd hi’ is her garden.
South Welsh shows having something with ‘gyda’: ‘gyda ni’ literally with us is how you say we have.
‘i’ (to) soft-mutates the word after it: ‘Caerdydd’ becomes ‘Gaerdydd’. ‘i Gaerdydd’ = to Cardiff.
‘fy’ nasal-mutates ‘c’ into ‘ngh’: ‘cefnder’ becomes ‘nghefnder’ in ‘fy nghefnder’, my cousin.
Comparatives usually add ‘-ach’ and take ‘na’ or ‘nag’: ‘bwysicach nag iechyd’ means more important than health.
Soft mutation can delete ‘g’ entirely: ‘gyrfa’ (career) becomes ‘ei yrfa’ (his career).
‘dy’ (your, informal) softens the next word: ‘cyfraniad’ becomes ‘dy gyfraniad’.
‘ei’ (her) adds an h before a vowel: ‘amynedd’ becomes ‘hamynedd’ in ‘ei hamynedd’, her patience.
Negative past can use aspirate mutation plus ‘ddim’: ‘clywais’ becomes ‘chlywais i ddim’ (I didn’t hear).
‘pan’ (when) soft-mutates the verb after it: ‘cnociodd’ becomes ‘gnociodd’. ‘pan gnociodd’ = when someone knocked.
Negatives usually soft-mutate the verb and add ‘ddim’: ‘ddwedodd hi ddim’ = she did not say, from ‘dwedodd’.
‘eu’ (their) causes no mutation: ‘eu cefnogaeth’ keeps its ‘c’, unlike ‘ei’ (his) which would soften it.
Putting a phrase first then adding ‘sy’n’ gives emphasis: ‘fy modryb sy’n gwneud’ means it is my aunt who makes.
For that she was, Welsh uses ‘bod’: ‘ei bod hi mor hwyr’ = that she was so late.
South Welsh shows possession with ‘gyda’: ‘doedd dim amser gyda fi’ means I had no time.
‘pe’ opens an unreal past condition: ‘pe baen ni wedi gadael’ means if we had left.
‘ei’ (her) aspirate-mutates a following ‘t’ into ‘th’: ‘traed’ becomes ‘thraed’ in ‘ei thraed’, her toes.
‘dwy’ (feminine two) soft-mutates the noun after it: ‘gwlad’ becomes ‘wlad’ in ‘i’r ddwy wlad’, the two countries.
‘allen nhw’ = they could, from ‘gallu’ (be able). Add ‘ddim’ to make it negative: ‘allen nhw ddim’ = they couldn’t.
